source_read: PDF, pp. 427-433 (all pages read; the Figure on p. 428 and Tables 1-3 on pp. 429-431 checked on rendered pages at 300 dpi, the rest at 150 dpi)

claims.overstatement: No causal overstatement. Wording points: (1) the opening sentence counts the twins' outcome among 'lifetime drug use disorders', but for drugs this study's abuse/dependence is a simplified symptom count (abuse = either of 2 abuse symptoms; dependence = 2 or more of 4 dependence symptoms), asked only of people who used a drug at least monthly, which the authors say does not provide formal DSM-IV criteria (p. 429); only alcohol dependence used full DSM-IV criteria. 'Drug abuse or dependence as the study defined it' would be exact. (2) 'the twin who started early more often reported any illicit drug abuse or dependence': 'met the study's criteria for' is more exact than 'reported'. (3) 'no separate estimates for identical pairs' is right for what is printed; the paper says separate identical- and fraternal-pair analyses (with cut-offs of 15, 16 and 18) confirmed its conclusions but shows no numbers (p. 431), so 'none reported' would be exact. (4) 'factors that differ between co-twins, such as friends, were measured only in part' can be read as friends being partly measured; friends or peers were not measured at all (the within-pair covariates were early tobacco and alcohol use, conduct disorder, major depression and social anxiety).
claims.note: All Lynskey numbers in the statement and magnitude match the rendered pages (Figure and Methods p. 428; Table 2 p. 430). Recomputed: 2765/4010 = 69%; 74 + 62 = 136 identical and 84 + 91 = 175 fraternal pairs; 234 + 77 = 311; every Table 2 percentage = n/311. 'Lowered the odds ratios by up to about a fifth': largest fall 19.4% (sedative use 2.83 to 2.28); any drug abuse/dependence 11.6%, alcohol dependence 14.7%, cannabis abuse/dependence 8.0%, several unchanged; correct. '311 of the 407 discordant pairs': the concordance analysis (p. 430) counts 88 + 110 + 98 + 111 = 407 discordant same-sex pairs against 311 analysed (62 of 88 identical male, 74 of 98 identical female, 91 of 110 fraternal male, 84 of 111 fraternal female), with no explanation: confirmed. In addition, its 229 concordant pairs imply 2 x 229 + 407 = 865 early starters among complete same-sex pairs, more than the 861 early starters reported for all 6,265 people interviewed (p. 428 and Figure), so the concordance counts and the sample-flow figure cannot both be right. Other reporting points: the adjusted alcohol-dependence OR 1.85 (1.21-2.83) is printed identically in Table 2 (311 pairs; unadjusted 2.17) and Table 3 (234 pairs; unadjusted 2.03), so one is probably a copying error, and the claim's adjusted figure rests on Table 2; the Comment's ranges of 2.3- to 3.9-fold and 1.6- to 6.0-fold (p. 431) are those of Table 3 (234 pairs), not of the main analysis summarised in the abstract (2.1 to 5.2); the 17 people who began another drug before cannabis are said to have been excluded from the analyses (p. 430), yet every Table 2 percentage still uses 311; the 24.8% of twins said to report no lifetime cannabis use (p. 430) is 77 of 311 co-twins, i.e. 12.4% of the 622 twins. Where both twins had used cannabis (234 pairs) cannabis abuse/dependence was only marginal after adjustment (1.57, 0.98-2.52, P = .06; Table 3, p. 431).

anchors.locator: Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure (sample size and selection)
anchors.extracted: Young-adult cohort of the volunteer Australian Twin Register, born 1964-1971; one telephone interview 1996-2000, median age 30 (range 24-36). Of 4010 traced pairs both twins interviewed in 2765 (69% pairwise response), one twin in 735 (78% individual response); 6265 people; 861 (13.7%) began cannabis before 17; 311 of them (36.1%) from same-sex pairs whose co-twin had not used cannabis by 17: 74 female and 62 male identical, 84 female and 91 male fraternal pairs. Figure: 234 co-twins began at 17 or older, 77 never used cannabis.

anchors.locator: Methods > Measures of subsequent drug involvement: Lifetime drug abuse/dependence paragraph (begins p. 428) and Lifetime alcohol dependence paragraph
anchors.extracted: Drug abuse/dependence questions asked only of people using cannabis, sedatives, cocaine/stimulants or opioids at least monthly; abuse = either of 2 abuse symptoms, dependence = 2 or more of 4 dependence symptoms; not formal DSM-IV criteria (for cannabis, sensitivity 96.7% and specificity 94.6% against DSM-IV in earlier work); drug classes combined because of low prevalence. Alcohol dependence by full DSM-IV criteria (27.9% of women, 44.8% of men).

anchors.locator: Methods > Family, social and individual factors; Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Covariates: DSM-IV conduct disorder and major depression, a nondiagnostic social-anxiety measure, early tobacco use (36.6%) and early regular alcohol use (11.6%) before 17. Conditional logistic regression in discordant pairs; interactions of early use with zygosity and with sex not significant (P > .10), so identical and fraternal pairs and both sexes were pooled; backward stepwise selection with early cannabis use forced in.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (311 pairs), abuse/dependence and alcohol dependence rows
anchors.extracted: Early starter vs co-twin, lifetime prevalence, unadjusted conditional OR (95% CI), adjusted OR: cannabis abuse/dependence 45.7% vs 31.8%, 2.13 (1.45-3.13), 1.96 (1.25-3.09); sedatives 2.6% vs 1.0%, 2.67 (0.71-10.05); cocaine/stimulants 12.5% vs 4.5%, 4.13 (1.91-8.93), 3.98 (1.73-9.17); opioids 3.5% vs 1.0%, 3.67 (1.02-13.14); any illicit drug abuse/dependence 47.6% vs 32.8%, 2.24 (1.52-3.30), 1.98 (1.26-3.10); alcohol dependence 42.8% vs 29.6%, 2.17 (1.46-3.24), 1.85 (1.21-2.83).

Concordance for early cannabis use higher in identical than fraternal pairs: men 65 concordant and 88 discordant identical vs 59 and 110 fraternal pairs (chi-square 7.92, P = .005); women 61 and 98 vs 44 and 111 (7.80, P = .005). These discordant counts total 407, against the 311 analysed, without explanation.

anchors.locator: Results, numbered points 2 and 3 (3rd and 4th paragraphs)
anchors.extracted: Unadjusted ORs 2.1 to 5.2, all significant except sedative abuse/dependence; the authors call the effect of adjustment negligible; 9 of 10 outcomes still significant.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (234 pairs in which both twins used cannabis); Results > Analyses restricted to those reporting lifetime cannabis use (begins p. 430)
anchors.extracted: Cannabis abuse/dependence 51.7% vs 42.3%, 1.58 (1.05-2.37), adjusted 1.57 (0.98-2.52), P = .06; any illicit drug abuse/dependence 54.3% vs 42.7%, 1.75 (1.16-2.64), adjusted 1.76 (1.08-2.84); alcohol dependence 46.6% vs 33.8%, 2.03 (1.30-3.17), adjusted 1.85 (1.21-2.83), the same adjusted value and interval as in Table 2.

Separate identical- and fraternal-pair analyses with cut-offs 15, 16 and 18 said to confirm the conclusions (no numbers). Authors: results consistent with early cannabis use having a causal role; unshared environmental confounding judged less plausible; shared family background and, in identical pairs, genes cannot explain the association. Limitations: self-report, retrospective data, no ages at progression; age of first use asked before drug problems in the interview.

Authors say strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn solely from the associations shown and call for research in other cultures and with other designs, including evaluation of prevention efforts that delay cannabis onset.

claims.overstatement: None material. 'Between 2.3 and 5.2 after adjustment' (adjusted 2.28 to 5.15) and 'between 2.3 and 3.9 (unadjusted) in the 234 pairs' (2.33 to 3.92) are correct roundings. 'Not explained by what co-twins share, such as their upbringing' is right for the shared environment; for genes the pooled identical-plus-fraternal estimate controls only part of the genetic resemblance, which the claim's next clause (no separate identical-pair estimates) covers; 'no separate estimates' is right for what is printed (separate analyses are said to confirm the conclusions, p. 431, but no numbers are shown). 'Later use of other drugs': the 17 people who began another drug before cannabis were excluded (p. 430), so 'later' holds for the early starters.
claims.note: All numbers checked on the rendered Table 2 (p. 430) and Table 3 (p. 431): 47.9% vs 26.4% = 149/311 and 82/311; 4.19 (2.60-6.75); 5.15; 2.83; 2.57; adjusted 2.28, 5.15, 4.06, 2.34; in 234 pairs unadjusted 3.00, 3.92, 3.00, 2.33 (adjusted 3.33, 3.92, 3.05, 2.40). The authors' mechanisms (p. 432): pleasurable early experiences, lowered perceived risk and legal barriers, and access to other drugs through contact with dealers (citing lower cocaine use among people who used cannabis in the Netherlands than in the US); the claim's 'social setting of cannabis use and access to other drugs' matches the abstract's conclusion. Same reporting points as for the other claim apply (407 discordant pairs in the concordance analysis vs 311 analysed; 865 implied vs 861 reported early starters; the Comment's ranges come from Table 3).

anchors.extracted: Volunteer Australian Twin Register cohort born 1964-1971, interviewed once by telephone in 1996-2000 at median age 30; 311 same-sex pairs in which one twin began cannabis before 17 and the co-twin had not used it by 17 (136 identical, 175 fraternal); 234 co-twins began at 17 or later, 77 never used cannabis.

Early starter vs co-twin: sedatives 19.0% vs 8.4%, OR 2.83 (1.66-4.85), adjusted 2.28 (1.20-4.31); hallucinogens 35.4% vs 18.0%, 5.15 (2.85-9.33), adjusted 5.15; cocaine/stimulants 47.9% vs 26.4%, 4.19 (2.60-6.75), adjusted 4.06 (2.30-7.17); opioids 13.5% vs 6.4%, 2.57 (1.39-4.77), adjusted 2.34 (1.13-4.85).

anchors.locator: Results > Subsidiary analyses; Comment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Separate identical and fraternal analyses (cut-offs 15, 16, 18) said to confirm the conclusions, without numbers. Authors: consistent with a causal role; 2.3- to 3.9-fold odds of other drug use (the Table 3 range); unshared environmental influences judged less plausible because twins are reared together.

Possible mechanisms: pleasurable first experiences, reduced perceived risk and weaker legal deterrence, and access to other drugs through contact with dealers; strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn solely from these associations.

key_findings.note: Agreed that the Breslow-Day statistics cannot be recomputed: a plain chi-square on the printed concordant/discordant counts gives 1.94 (men) and 3.51 (women), so the test must use the unprinted pairs concordant for no early use.

Reconstruction re-done independently: every unadjusted OR and interval in Tables 2 and 3 is reproduced by b/c with b - c equal to the difference in printed counts (e.g. 67/13 hallucinogen use, 88/21 cocaine/stimulant use, 83/37 any drug abuse/dependence, 8/3 sedative abuse/dependence), to within rounding (4.125 printed 4.13; alcohol dependence lower limit 1.453 printed 1.46).

Small precision: the paper labels only the THC cross-tolerance studies as rat studies; the species of the dopamine study (ref. 37) is not stated in the paper, and the authors' counter-argument refers to exposures in 'laboratory-based research'. Substance unchanged.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in step 1 (Tables 2 and 3, adjusted alcohol dependence 1.85, 1.21-2.83, covariates 3 and 4 in both).

Recomputed: 0.125 x 0.875 / (0.045 x 0.955) = 2.55; the odds ratio for those prevalences is 3.03. That the formula's value equals the reported 2.5 threshold may be partly coincidental, since a minimum detectable OR should come from varying pE, but the printed formula is wrong either way.
88 + 110 + 98 + 111 = 407; identical discordant 88 + 98 = 186 vs 136 analysed (50 missing); 96/407 = 24% of discordant pairs. See missed item 1 for a further inconsistency in the same counts.

Checked: for none of the four drug classes does an integer split of the Table 2 totals give the Methods percentages with 306 men and 316 women; denominators of about 304 men and 312-315 women fit, consistent with some people being dropped.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high: the co-twin design removes shared rearing and part of genetic confounding, but non-shared factors (peers, temperament) were not measured, fraternal pairs are pooled with identical pairs, and covariates were recalled at about 30 and chosen stepwise.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the authors themselves say strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn (p. 432) and hedge the mechanisms with 'may'. The weakest point is the abstract's statement that common genetic factors cannot solely explain the association, which rests on a non-significant zygosity interaction and unreported identical-pair estimates, with 50 identical discordant pairs not analysed; the title's 'escalation' and the closing call for interventions to prevent escalation (p. 432, last paragraph of the Comment) rest on lifetime prevalences without ages at progression.

missed: The concordance counts are internally inconsistent with the sample-flow figure: 229 concordant pairs (65 + 59 + 61 + 44) contribute 458 early starters and the 407 discordant pairs 407 more, i.e. 865 early starters among complete same-sex pairs (p. 430), but the whole interviewed sample had only 861 early starters (p. 428, Figure), before counting singletons and opposite-sex pairs. The concordance analysis and the analysed sample therefore cannot both be counted as printed; this strengthens reporting issue 2.

can_establish says the early starter more often reported 'later' alcohol dependence; the paper has no ages at onset of problems (p. 431 limitation), so for alcohol dependence (and abuse/dependence generally) only the lifetime difference, not its timing relative to early cannabis use, is shown. For other drug use, 'later' holds by construction because the 17 people who started another drug first were excluded.
